To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the following two statements are true: (a) The probability that a sample of size $N$ is complete (i.e. contains no missing observations) is $p_N$, where $p_N=1-\left(\frac{1}{N}\right)^{1/\alpha}$, and $\alpha$ is the number of distinct observations in the sample (i.e. the number of different values of $x$).
the sample size of a random sample is not a random variable, and the sample size of an incomplete sample is also not random, but is a random variable.

(1) The sample size of a single sample can be estimated by a method based on the observed sample mean, and (2) When more than one complete sample is available, then the sample size of each sample can be estimated, and the relative sizes of the samples can be estimated as well.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following problem: Suppose a random sample is to be taken from a population having a distribution which is known only in a very limited degree. What is the best size of the sample to be taken?

the analysis of random samples, with special emphasis on the analysis of possibly incomplete samples and with the analysis of sets of samples, and with methods which can be applied when the distribution(s) are not known.
the problem of making statistical inferences from possibly incomplete random samples, and with the problem of estimating the sample size of such a sample.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, if a set of samples is available, and the number of samples is not too large, then a more thorough investigation of the field of hypotheses is warranted than if only a single sample were available.
, for any given problem, the most appropriate statistical analysis depends on the nature of the problem and on the data available.
the methods of this paper, as well as those of earlier papers, provide the means for making inferences on sample size.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, given a random sample, we can make inferences on the size of the population, the size of the sample and the completeness of the sample.

the methods developed here and in earlier papers provide a basis for analysis of incomplete data, when the distribution(s) is (are) known, and also for the analysis of data when the distribution is not known, and when the data are incomplete.
the methods developed in the present paper and the earlier papers provide the basis for a general approach to statistical problems which is not limited to the usual case of complete samples.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the analysis of incomplete random samples is a rich and fruitful area for further research.
, when the data are not completely known, the field of possible inferences is much wider than that when the data are completely observed.
the analysis of a single sample can often be extended to a sequence of samples, and that the resulting analyses can often be more informative than those of a single sample.
